title: Good Man Wang: Do Not Blame Others (Audio)
author: Wang Fengyi
excerpt: A golden saying of nine words: Do not blame others; find the good; acknowledge your faults.

inline.s: (Excerpted from
Wang Fengyi's Record of Excellent Sayings
A golden saying of nine words: Do not blame others; find the good; acknowledge your faults.

I have often pondered: to blame others is a sea of suffering. The more you blame others, the more wretched your heart grows, until you either fall ill or invite calamity — is this not a sea of suffering? To manage others is a hell: manage them a tenth and they resent you a tenth; manage them fully and they resent you fully — is this not a hell? One must turn it around. Only one who can guide others can settle the debts of human life and fulfill the way of being human. One who can ferry others across is a spirit; one who can perfect others is a Buddha.

The noble person seeks within himself; the petty person seeks from others. When the noble person lacks virtue, he blames himself and cultivates himself; when the petty person has faults, he blames others. He does not blame with his mouth but blames in his heart, and the more he blames the more wretched his heart grows. The grievance that is kept in the heart is poisonous; stored there it not only brings misery but also causes illness — it is in effect swallowing poison oneself. If one can reflect and find one's own faults, one will naturally cease to blame outward. If you are able, do not blame the unable; if you know, do not blame the ignorant. One who understands the way of facing people will not blame others.

People today are unhappy because others look down on them. But as for me, good is good and bad is bad; what matter whether others think well of me? Just this one thing, not blaming others, is enough to become a Buddha. The clever people of today are forever calculating; and when they tally it up it is either regret or grievance — how can they not fall ill?
The three words “do not blame others” are wonderfully perfect!

blocks.text: 2. Do Not Give Way to Anger or the Fire of Temper

inline.s: I have often pondered: when fire runs backward one spits blood; when anger runs backward one vomits food. If one can practice the Way and understand the Way, then anger and fire both subside.

A rising temper is the “dragon's croon”; anger is the “tiger's roar.” Only one who can subdue his temper and fire can perfect the Way. When someone provokes you, do not get angry; if you get angry, the anger sinks and turns to cold. When circumstances press you, do not grow anxious; if you grow anxious, the fire rises and turns to heat. Both cold and heat can harm a person. The cultivator is not elated by good fortune nor anxious at ill fortune; then temper and fire do not arise at all — this is “subduing the dragon and taming the tiger.” If one can subdue them, they serve me; if one cannot, they become a demon.

When one's innate nature is in command, the ghost comes to rule the house. Because anger and rising temper surely bring illness, and falling ill is being struck down by a ghost! When right thought arises, the spirit arrives; when a wrong thought arises, the ghost is present. It is a pity that people will not be a spirit but are content to be a ghost!

Fire arises from the heart; as soon as the heart stirs, fire is born. The moment one grows anxious, fire rises; the moment a thought is set in motion, fire scatters outward. If one can still the heart, the fire sinks of itself. For one who does not keep to his own lot, with its extra cravings, the fire is set in reckless motion. If one can let the heart go and not grow anxious on behalf of others, then the fire does not arise — how light and free that would be!

Stirring one's nature (throwing a tantrum) is fire; being angry at heart is anger as such. The Buddha spoke of “examining the mind in seven places,” but I say one must kill off the human heart altogether. When the human heart dies, the mind of the Way is born of itself; when the human heart stirs, the mind of the Way is extinguished of itself, and the thought of contention and greed arises. Because of contention one becomes angry; because of greed one's temper flares. Anger and fire attack the heart, and one frets all day long. Even wealth and honor bring no pleasure then. So the ancients treated the heart as one treats illness. I say, kill off the heart — how much trouble that saves!

blocks.text: 3. Find the Good, Acknowledge Your Faults

inline.s: Many are those who cultivate goodness, yet few gain its benefits. Why is that? Simply because in their hearts they store only the faults of others — how can they then obtain good?

Finding others' good is “gathering the spirit”; noticing others' faults is “collecting the spoils.” To “gather the spirit” is to gather the sunlight, warming the heart and nourishing it; to “collect the spoils” is to store up dark energy, making the heart gloomy and so harming the body. Everyone has good points — even a wicked person has good points. If you cannot find them on the positive side, look for them on the shadow side. Therefore I say that finding the good is a “pill that warms the heart.” Wherever you go you will have good connections, and you will be forever free of sorrow.

Finding the good is true gold. If you wish to find the good, you must make resolve your root; amid what holds not a trace of good, you must find the genuine good. When you have reached the point where you can bear it no longer, yet still can bear it — this is “great righteousness reaching to heaven.”

Acknowledging one's faults gives rise to the water of wisdom. Water can blend the five flavors and harmonize the five colors, taking the square or the round as it finds them. If one can train one's nature to be like water, one has perfected the Way. Hence the ancients said: “The highest good is like water.”

Man is one body with heaven and earth; all the affairs of the world are one's own concern. If the world has not become good, how can we be without fault? Fault is everywhere: when you bow your head, there it is; when you lift your head, there it is; with your eyes open it is there; with your eyes closed it is there. To see that your wife is not good — that is fault found with lowered head. To see that your elders are wrong — that is fault found with lifted head. To see that others are wrong — that is fault found with open eyes. To ponder in your heart that others are wrong — that is fault found with closed eyes. As I see it, whatever way you do not understand, whatever task you cannot do — that is all fault. If one can find one's own lot, then one will know one's faults. People have lost the principle of heaven, are confused about the course of things, and have wronged their fellow feeling — and still do not know to acknowledge their faults.
If one can truly own one's faults, then naturally the spirit is clear and the breath refreshed, and the heart is calm and the temper composed.
Acknowledging faults gives birth to the water of wisdom; finding the good gives birth to the ringing gold.
Finding the good opens the road to heaven; acknowledging faults closes the gate of hell.
Acknowledging faults is better than taking a “cooling powder”; finding the good is better than using the “pill that warms the heart.”
